text.p: A firmer dollar after U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan opened a testimony kept the gold market on the defensive on Tuesday, dealers said.
Greenspan began his address to the Senate Budget Committee as gold entered a short-covering rally which probed $355.00 per ounce, the top of its recent tight trading range.
But comments that U.S. inflation was slower than anticipated, and growth faster, boosted the dollar and gold eased back to fix at $354.70, still up $1.30 from the morning setting.
"We only expected Greenspan to have an impact if he said something directly relevant," one bullion dealer said.
Shortly after the fixing the Comex February contract was about $0.50 ahead at $355.10, over a dollar under its earlier intra day high.
"The dollar has definitely been affecting gold which hasn't happened for a while," the dealer said.

"The reason is that with the dollar strong and gold so weak, it's very attractive to sell gold. There are big chart points at 4180 for gold in yen and 501 in Swiss Francs and they're around there right now," he said.
Earlier, gold"s upside was held by what one dealer described as "quality selling".
"The selling looks like it could be from a producer or an institution. But it surprising to see it at these levels,' he said.
Selling was evident at around $353.35 in early European, late Asian trading, the dealer said.
He noted that the market had been as low as $351.10/$351.40 but had held around $352.00 overnight while running into selling at $354.00.
"That is getting into a very narrow range. We are so close to $350.00, that we may have to go down and look at it even if the price bounces again very quickly," he said.
However he added there was also the chance of a "wash out" taking the price lower than that.

Platinum recovered from a fresh recent low fix in the morning to $348.25/$359.25, down just 25 cents from the previous close by 1530 GMT. "Platinum is suffering due to the stronger dollar and the slumping Japanese stock market," a dealer said.

Palladium took some support from the continuing lack of dialogue between Russian exporters and Japanese importers of the metal on 1997 delivery contracts. It was 50 cents up on the close at $121.50/$122.50.
"Option buying in silver looks to have pushed up prices," a dealer said as silver briefly nudged $4.78/$4.80, the day's high.
But by 1545 GMT it had eased with gold to $4.76/$4.78, still three cents ahead.
